articleHtml:
By David Vance, Senior Financial Modeler & SmartCalcLab Review Board · Last updated: November 27, 2026

The three questions behind every percentage problem

Almost every percentage problem is one of three questions: what is X% of Y, what percent is X of Y, or how much did a value change in percent. The calculator above handles all three. The harder part is knowing which question you are actually asking, and that is where most mistakes happen. Here are the formulas, then the traps.

Core formulas with examples

  • X% of Y: Y × X ÷ 100. Example: 18% tip on $64.50 = 64.50 × 0.18 = $11.61.
  • What percent is A of B: A ÷ B × 100. Example: you scored 42 out of 60, so 42 ÷ 60 × 100 = 70%.
  • Percent change: (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Example: rent goes from $1,200 to $1,320, so (1,320 − 1,200) ÷ 1,200 = +10%.

Note that percent change is always measured against the old value. That detail explains the next surprise.

Trap 1: up 50%, down 50% does not bring you back

A price of $100 rises 50% to $150. A fall of 50% from $150 takes off $75 and leaves $75, a net loss of 25%. The same happens to an investment: a 50% loss needs a 100% gain to recover. Gains and losses are measured against different bases.

Trap 2: stacked discounts do not add

A shop advertises "30% off, then an extra 20% off". Many people assume 50%. The second discount applies to the already reduced price: 100 × 0.70 × 0.80 = 56. The total discount is 44%. The general rule: multiply the remaining fractions, then subtract from 1. Two discounts of 25% give 1 − 0.75 × 0.75 = 43.75%.

Trap 3: working backwards from a discounted price

An item costs $120 after a 20% discount. What was the original price? Adding 20% to $120 gives $144, which is wrong. The $120 is 80% of the original, so divide: 120 ÷ 0.80 = $150. The same logic works for any sale: $85 after 15% off came from 85 ÷ 0.85 = $100.

GST and VAT: adding and removing tax

Suppose a bill is ₹1,000 plus 18% GST. Adding tax is easy: 1,000 × 1.18 = ₹1,180. Taking tax out of a total is where people slip. From a ₹1,180 invoice, do not compute 18% of 1,180 (₹212.40). Divide by 1.18 to get the pre-tax price, ₹1,000, then the tax is ₹180. The same method works for VAT or sales tax shown inside a price.

Add 18% GST to ₹1,0001,000 × 1.18₹1,180
Remove 18% GST from ₹1,1801,180 ÷ 1.18₹1,000
Wrong: subtract 18% of ₹1,1801,180 − 212.40₹967.60

Percent vs percentage points

If an interest rate moves from 5% to 6%, it has risen by 1 percentage point, but by 20 percent in relative terms (1 ÷ 5). News reports often mix the two. When a headline says "unemployment rose 2%", check whether it means 2 points or 2 percent of the previous rate.

Margin vs markup

A shop buys a product for $80 and sells it for $100. The profit is $20. Markup is profit over cost: 20 ÷ 80 = 25%. Margin is profit over selling price: 20 ÷ 100 = 20%. They are both correct but different. Always check which one a supplier or colleague is quoting.

Quick mental shortcuts

  • 10%: move the decimal one place left. 10% of 64.50 is 6.45.
  • 5%: half of 10%. 5% of 64.50 is about 3.23.
  • 15% tip: 10% plus 5%. For 64.50 that is 6.45 + 3.23 ≈ 9.68.
  • 1%: move the decimal two places left, then multiply for other percentages.
  • X% of Y equals Y% of X: 8% of 50 is the same as 50% of 8, which is 4. Use the easier one.

Where percentages appear in daily money decisions

  • Shopping: compare "40% off" with "buy one, get one 50% off". On two $50 items the first costs $60 and the second $75.
  • Salary: a 6% raise on $50,000 is $3,000, but you keep less after tax.
  • Loans: see the effect of an extra 1% on interest in our loan calculator.
  • Exams and grading: a weighted average uses percentages as weights, not simple averages.

Common mistakes

  • Using the new value as the base for percent change.
  • Adding discounts together instead of multiplying them.
  • Subtracting a percentage of the total when removing tax.
  • Comparing percentages of different bases, such as 20% of a small number with 10% of a large one.
  • Reporting a change in percentage points as a percent.

Frequently asked questions

How do I calculate percentage increase?

Subtract the old value from the new value, divide by the old value, then multiply by 100. For 50 rising to 65 the increase is (65 − 50) ÷ 50 × 100 = 30%.

How do I find the original price before a discount?

Divide the sale price by the fraction you paid. If a 20% discount led to $120, divide by 0.80 to get the original price of $150.

Why do two 25% discounts not make 50%?

The second discount applies to the reduced price. After the first discount you pay 75%, and 75% of 75% is 56.25%, so the total discount is 43.75%.

What is the difference between percent and percentage points?

A percentage point is the arithmetic difference between two percentages, while percent change compares them proportionally. A move from 5% to 6% is 1 percentage point or a 20% relative increase.

Methodology and sources

All calculations use standard arithmetic and are rounded to two decimals where shown. GST examples use an 18% rate for illustration; check the rate that applies to your goods or services. Corrections: support@smartcalclab.com.
